chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Umar ibn Udhaynahh, from Aban ibn Abi Ayyash, from Sulaym ibn Qays al-Hilali who said:

I heard the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) narrating from the Prophet (may God's blessings be upon him and his family) that he said in a speech of his: The scholars are two (types of) men — a scholar who acts upon his knowledge, and this one is saved; and a scholar who neglects his knowledge, and this one is destroyed.
The inhabitants of the Fire will surely be harmed by the stench of the scholar who neglected his knowledge.

And the one with the most intense remorse and anguish among the inhabitants of the Fire will be a man who invited a servant toward God, and he answered him and accepted from him, and so he obeyed God, and God admitted him into Paradise — but admitted the inviter into the Fire because of his abandoning his knowledge, his following of personal desires, and prolonged worldly ambitions.
As for following personal desires, it blocks one from the Truth; and prolonged worldly ambitions cause one to forget the Hereafter.

key_terms.الداعي: The da'i — the one who calls/invites others to God; here a tragic figure of spiritual failure
key_terms.العالم التارك لعلمه: The scholar who abandons his knowledge — a recurring theme in hadith about hypocrisy and accountability
key_terms.الهوى: Hawa — personal desires, whims, or passions that pull one away from divine guidance
key_terms.طول الأمل: Tul al-Amal — prolonged worldly hopes or ambitions that distract from the Hereafter

ai.seo_question: What is the punishment for scholars who do not act on their knowledge in Islam?
ai.summary: The Prophet (SAWW) through Imam Ali (AS) classifies scholars into two contrasting types: those who act on their knowledge and are saved, and those who abandon it and are destroyed. The narration reaches its most sobering point with the figure of the da'i — a man who guided someone else to God and Paradise, yet entered the Fire himself because he failed to act on his own knowledge and succumbed to worldly desires and ambitions. This teaching was directed at early Muslim communities where religious scholarship carried immense social status, cautioning that knowledge without practice is not only useless but actively damning.
